# The Coronary Slow Flow Phenomenon: A Narrative Review

The coronary slow flow phenomenon (CSFP) is an angiographic entity first described by Tambe et al. in 1972 [1]. It is characterized by delayed distal vessel opacification of contrast medium in epicardial coronary arteries without evidence of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD). For decades, CSFP was considered a benign angiographic curiosity. However, contemporary evidence demonstrates that it is clinically significant and associated with recurrent angina, myocardial ischemia, life-threatening arrhythmias, and even sudden cardiac death [2,3]. Historically, the definition of slow flow was highly subjective. This changed when Gibson et al. introduced the Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction (TIMI) frame count (TFC), establishing a quantitative, reproducible method to evaluate coronary blood flow velocity [2]. Utilizing a corrected TFC (cTFC) threshold greater than 27 frames for the left anterior descending artery, clinicians can reliably distinguish CSFP from normal flow [2,4].

Unlike traditional CAD, which predominantly affects older individuals with classic cardiovascular risk factors, CSFP has a unique demographic footprint [4]. It typically presents in younger male patients, often active smokers, who present to the emergency department with acute-onset chest pain mimicking acute coronary syndrome (ACS) [4,5]. In fact, up to 4% of patients undergoing diagnostic coronary angiography for suspected CAD are found to have CSFP [5]. While often presenting with atypical angina, these patients suffer from a significantly impaired quality of life and undergo frequent re-hospitalizations due to recurrent chest pain [6].

The exact pathophysiology of CSFP remains enigmatic and is likely multifactorial. Initial histological studies by Mangieri et al. on myocardial biopsies of affected patients revealed fibromuscular hyperplasia, medial hypertrophy, and endothelial swelling in the coronary microcirculation, suggesting primary microvascular dysfunction [5]. To better understand epicardial vessel involvement, intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) have been utilized. Pekdemir et al. [7] and Cin et al. [8] demonstrated diffuse intimal thickening and subclinical non-obstructive atherosclerosis in the epicardial vessels of CSFP patients. This was further substantiated by high-resolution OCT findings demonstrating eccentric plaques and positive remodeling even in angiographically "normal" arteries [9].

In addition to structural alterations, functional endothelial dysfunction plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of CSFP [10]. Impaired flow-mediated dilation of the brachial artery highlights that CSFP may represent a manifestation of generalized endothelial and microvascular dysfunction [10]. This systemic impairment is closely linked to chronic low-grade inflammation. Elevated levels of cell adhesion molecules (such as ICAM-1, VCAM-1, and E-selectin) [11], pro-inflammatory cytokines [12], and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) [13] have been consistently observed in patients with CSFP, underscoring the role of inflammatory pathways.

Given its complex etiology, the management of CSFP remains challenging. Conventional anti-anginal medications such as beta-blockers and nitrates often yield suboptimal results. However, targeted therapies addressing microvascular tone and endothelial function have shown promise. Nitric oxide (NO)-modulating beta-blockers, such as nebivolol, have been shown to improve both coronary flow velocity and coronary flow reserve, as well as alleviate anginal symptoms [14,15]. Calcium channel blockers, particularly diltiazem, have also demonstrated efficacy in reducing TFC and improving exercise tolerance, likely by mitigating microvascular spasm [16,17].

In light of the chronic inflammatory status and subclinical atherosclerosis underlying CSFP, statin therapy has emerged as a cornerstone of management. Atorvastatin therapy has been shown to reduce inflammatory markers and significantly improve coronary flow, as measured by TFC [18,19]. Furthermore, autonomic nervous system imbalance, marked by reduced heart rate variability, has been identified in CSFP patients, suggesting that neurohumoral modulation may be another potential therapeutic target [20].

Though initially deemed a benign condition, long-term follow-up studies paint a more guarded picture [21,22]. While the risk of hard cardiovascular end-points (such as myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death) is lower than in obstructive CAD, patients experience persistent symptoms, recurrent hospital admissions, and a notable incidence of ventricular arrhythmias [23,24,25]. A comprehensive understanding of CSFP requires recognizing it as a systemic microcirculatory disorder rather than an isolated cardiac anomaly [26,27]. Future research must focus on large-scale randomized controlled trials to establish standardized, evidence-based guidelines for this frequently overlooked clinical entity [28,29,30].
